entries.95cf7e2dda647c730a9f72173bc4e780120c92de: <div sID="gen5741" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="23" osisID="1Sam.23" sID="1Sam.23"/> <div eID="gen5741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5742" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen5743" type="x-p"/> Saul, having made himself drunk with the blood of the priests of the Lord, is here, in this chapter, seeking David's life, who appears here doing good, and suffering ill, at the same time. Here is, I. The good service he did to his king and country, in rescuing the city of Keilah out of the hands of the Philistines, <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.1-1Sam.23.6">ver. 1-6</reference>. II. The danger he was thereby brought into from the malice of the prince he served and the treachery of the city he saved, and his deliverance, by divine direction, from that danger, <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.7-1Sam.23.13">ver. 7-13</reference>. III. David in a wood and his friend Jonathan visiting him there and encouraging him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.14-1Sam.23.18">ver. 14-18</reference>. IV. The information which the Ziphites brought to Saul of David's haunts, and the expedition Saul made, in pursuit of him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.19-1Sam.23.25">ver. 19-25</reference>. The narrow escape David had of falling into his hands, <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.26-1Sam.23.29">ver. 26-29</reference>. "Many are the troubles of the righteous, but the Lord delivereth them out of them all."
entries.74b7de818d5cc2d89b34cf7d583a67682013fbdc: <div eID="gen5743" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen5742" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">David Delivers Keilah. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1057.)</title> <div sID="gen5744" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Then they told David, saying, Behold, the Philistines fight against Keilah, and they rob the threshingfloors. <hi type="super">2</hi> Therefore David enquired of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , saying, Shall I go and smite these Philistines? And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto David, Go, and smite the Philistines, and save Keilah. <hi type="super">3</hi> And David's men said unto him, Behold, we be afraid here in Judah: how much more then if we come to Keilah against the armies of the Philistines? <hi type="super">4</hi> Then David enquired of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> yet again. And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> answered him and said, Arise, go down to Keilah; for I will deliver the Philistines into thine hand. <hi type="super">5</hi> So David and his men went to Keilah, and fought with the Philistines, and brought away their cattle, and smote them with a great slaughter. So David saved the inhabitants of Keilah. <hi type="super">6</hi> And it came to pass, when Abiathar the son of Ahimelech fled to David to Keilah, <hi type="italic">that</hi> he came down <hi type="italic">with</hi> an ephod in his hand. <div eID="gen5744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5745" type="x-p"/> Now we find why the prophet Gad (by divine direction, no doubt) ordered David to go into the land of Judah, <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.5">ch. xxii. 5</reference>. It was that, since Saul neglected the public safety, he might take care of it, notwithstanding the ill treatment that was given him; for he must render good for evil, and therein be a type of him who not only ventured his life, but laid down his life, for those that were his enemies. <div eID="gen5745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5746" type="x-p"/> I. Tidings are brought to David, as to the patron and protector of his country's liberties, that the Philistines had made a descent upon the city of Keilah and plundered the country thereabouts, <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.1">v. 1</reference>. Probably it was the departure both of God and David from Saul that encouraged the Philistines to make this incursion. When princes begin to persecute God's people and ministers, let them expect no other than vexation on all sides. The way for any country to be quiet is to let God's church be quiet in it. If Saul fight against David, the Philistines shall fight against his country. <div eID="gen5746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5747" type="x-p"/> II. David is forward enough to come in for their relief, but is willing to enquire of the Lord concerning it. Here is an instance, 1. Of David's generosity and public-spiritedness. Though his head and hands were full of his own business, and he had enough to do, with the little force he had, to secure himself, yet he was concerned for the safety of his country and could not sit still to see that ravaged: nay, though Saul, whose business it was to guard the borders of his land, hated him and sought his life, yet he was willing, to the utmost of his power, to serve him and his interests against the common enemy, and bravely abhorred the thought of sacrificing the common welfare to his private revenge. Those are unlike to David who sullenly decline to do good because they have not been so well considered as they deserved for the services they have done. 2. Of David's piety and regard to God. He enquired of the Lord by the prophet Gad; for it should seem (by <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.6">v. 6</reference>) that Abiathar came not to him with the ephod till he was in Keilah. His enquiry is, <hi type="italic">Shall I go and smite these Philistines?</hi> He enquires both concerning the duty (whether he might lawfully take Saul's work out of his hand, and act without a commission from him) and concerning the event, whether he might safely venture against such a force as the Philistines had with such a handful of men at his feet, and such a dangerous enemy as Saul was at his back. It is our duty, and will be our case and comfort, whatever happens, to acknowledge God in all our ways and to seek direction from him. <div eID="gen5747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5748" type="x-p"/> III. God appointed him once and again to go against the Philistines, and promised him success: <hi type="italic">Go, and smite the Philistines,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.2">v. 2</reference>. His men opposed it, <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.3">v. 3</reference>. No sooner did he begin to have soldiers of his own than he found it hard enough to manage them. They objected that they had enemies enough among their own countrymen, they needed not to make the Philistines their enemies. Their hearts failed them when they only apprehended themselves in danger from Saul's band of pursuers, much more when they came to engage the Philistine-armies. To satisfy them, therefore, he <hi type="italic">enquired of the Lord again,</hi> and now received, not only a full commission, which would warrant him to fight though he had no orders from Saul (<hi type="italic">Arise, go down to Keilah</hi>), but also a full assurance of victory: <hi type="italic">I will deliver the Philistines into thy hand,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.4">v. 4</reference>. This was enough to animate the greatest coward he had in his regiment. <div eID="gen5748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5749" type="x-p"/> IV. He went accordingly against the Philistines, routed them, and rescued Keilah, (<reference osisRef="1Sam.23.5">v. 5</reference>), and it should seem he made a sally into the country of the Philistines, for he carried off their cattle by way of reprisal for the wrong they did to the men of Keilah in robbing their threshing-floors. Here notice is taken (<reference osisRef="1Sam.23.6">v. 6</reference>) that it was while David remained in Keilah, after he had cleared it of the Philistines, that Abiathar came to him with the ephod in his hand, that is, the high priest's ephod, in which the urim and thummim were. It was a great comfort to David, in his banishment, that when he could not go to the house of God he had some of the choicest treasures of that house brought to him, the high priest and his breast-plate of judgment.
entries.280718ad74bb0ffb9cbcccf300da7df4becc30c4: <div eID="gen5749" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">David Escapes from Keilah. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1057.)</title> <div sID="gen5750" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> And it was told Saul that David was come to Keilah. And Saul said, God hath delivered him into mine hand; for he is shut in, by entering into a town that hath gates and bars. <hi type="super">8</hi> And Saul called all the people together to war, to go down to Keilah, to besiege David and his men. <hi type="super">9</hi> And David knew that Saul secretly practised mischief against him; and he said to Abiathar the priest, Bring hither the ephod. <hi type="super">10</hi> Then said David, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> God of Israel, thy servant hath certainly heard that Saul seeketh to come to Keilah, to destroy the city for my sake. <hi type="super">11</hi> Will the men of Keilah deliver me up into his hand? will Saul come down, as thy servant hath heard? <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> God of Israel, I beseech thee, tell thy servant. And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said, He will come down. <hi type="super">12</hi> Then said David, Will the men of Keilah deliver me and my men into the hand of Saul? And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said, They will deliver <hi type="italic">thee</hi> up. <hi type="super">13</hi> Then David and his men, <hi type="italic">which were</hi> about six hundred, arose and departed out of Keilah, and went whithersoever they could go. And it was told Saul that David was escaped from Keilah; and he forbare to go forth. <div eID="gen5750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5751" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. Saul contriving within himself the destruction of David (<reference osisRef="1Sam.23.7-1Sam.23.8">v. 7, 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">He heard that he had come to Keilah;</hi> and did he not hear what brought him thither? Was it not told him that he had bravely relieved Keilah and delivered it out of the hands of the Philistines? This, one would think, should have put Saul upon considering what honour and dignity should be done to David for this. But, instead of that, he catches at it as an opportunity of doing David a mischief. An ungrateful wretch he was, and for ever unworthy to have any service or kindness done him. Well might David complain of his enemies that they rewarded him <hi type="italic">evil for good,</hi> and that for his love they were his adversaries, <reference osisRef="Ps.35.12">Ps. xxxv. 12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.109.4">cix. 4</reference>. Christ was used thus basely, <reference osisRef="John.10.32">John x. 32</reference>. Now observe, 1. How Saul abused the <hi type="italic">God of Israel,</hi> in making his providence to patronise and give countenance to his malicious designs, and thence promising himself success in them: <hi type="italic">God hath delivered him into my hand;</hi> as if he who was rejected of God were in this instance owned and favoured by him, and David infatuated. He vainly triumphs before the victory, forgetting how often he had had fairer advantages against David than he had now and had yet missed his aim. He impiously connects God with his cause, because he thought he had gained one point. Therefore David prays (<reference osisRef="Ps.140.8">Ps. cxl. 8</reference>), <hi type="italic">Grant not, O Lord! the desires of the wicked; further not his wicked device, lest they exalt themselves.</hi> We must not think that one smiling providence either justifies an unrighteous cause or secures its success. 2. How Saul abused the Israel of God, in making them the servants of his malice against David. He called all the people together to war, and they must with all speed march to Keilah, pretending to oppose the Philistines, but intending to besiege David and his men, though concealing that design; for it is said (<reference osisRef="1Sam.23.9">v. 9</reference>) that he <hi type="italic">secretly practised mischief against him.</hi> Miserable is that people whose prince is a tyrant, for, while some are sufferers by his tyranny, others (which is worse) are made servants to it and instruments of it. <div eID="gen5751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5752" type="x-p"/> II. David consulting with God concerning his own preservation. He knew by the information bought him that Saul was plotting his ruin (<reference osisRef="1Sam.23.9">v. 9</reference>) and therefore applied to his great protector for direction. No sooner is the ephod brought to him than he makes use of it: <hi type="italic">Bring hither the ephod.</hi> We have the scriptures, those lively oracles, in our hands; let us take advice from them in doubtful cases. "Bring hither the Bible." <div eID="gen5752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5753" type="x-p"/> 1. David's address to God upon this occasion is, (1.) Very solemn and reverent. Twice he calls God the <hi type="italic">Lord God of Israel,</hi> and thrice calls himself his <hi type="italic">servant,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.10-1Sam.23.11">v. 10, 11</reference>. Those that address God must know their distance, and who they are speaking to. (2.) Very particular and express. His representation of the case is so (<reference osisRef="1Sam.23.10">v. 10</reference>): "Thy servant has certainly heard on good authority" (for he would not call for the ephod upon every idle rumour) "that Saul has a design upon Keilah;" he does not say, "to destroy me," but, "to destroy the city" (as he had lately done the city of Nob) "for my sake." He seems more solicitous for their safety than for his own, and will expose himself any where rather than they shall be brought into trouble by his being among them. Generous souls are thus minded. His queries upon the case are likewise very particular. God allows us to be so in our addresses to him: "Lord, direct me in this matter, about which I am now at a loss." He does indeed invert the due order of his queries, but God in his answer puts him into method. That question should have been put first, and was first answered, "Will Saul come down, as thy servant has heard?" "Yea," says the oracle, "he will come down; he has resolved it, is preparing for it, and will do it, unless he hear that thou hast quitted the town." "Well, but if he do come down will the men of Keilah stand by me in holding the city against him, or will they open to him the gates, and deliver me into his hand?" If he had asked the men (the magistrates or elders) of Keilah themselves what they would do in that case, they could not have told him, not knowing their own minds, nor what they should do when it came to the trial, much less which way the superior vote of their council would carry it; or they might have told him they would protect him, and yet afterwards have betrayed him; but God could tell him infallibly: "When Saul besieges their city, and demands of them that they surrender thee into his hands, how fond soever they now seem of thee, as their saviour, they will deliver thee up rather than stand the shock of Saul's fury." Note, [1.] God knows all men better than they know themselves, knows their length, their strength, what is in them, and what they will do if they come into such and such circumstances. [2.] He therefore knows not only what <hi type="italic">will</hi> be, but what <hi type="italic">would</hi> be if it were not prevented; and therefore knows how to deliver the godly out of temptation, and how to render to every man according to his works. <div eID="gen5753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5754" type="x-p"/> 2. David, having thus far notice given him of his danger, quitted Keilah, <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.13">v. 13</reference>. His followers had now increased in number to 600; with these he went out, not knowing whither he went, but resolving to follow Providence and put himself under its protection. This broke Saul's measures. He thought God had delivered David into his hand, but it proved that God delivered him out of his hand, as a bird out of the snare of the fowler. When <hi type="italic">Saul heard that David had escaped from Keilah, he forbore to go forth</hi> with the body of the army, as he intended (<reference osisRef="1Sam.23.8">v. 8</reference>), and resolved to take only his own guards, and go in quest of his people's enemies and turn their counsels head-long.
entries.e872c53ba1346323ba1b7353035683f7d6ecc2bb: <div eID="gen5754" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">David in the Wilderness of Ziph. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1057.)</title> <div sID="gen5755" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> And David abode in the wilderness in strong holds, and remained in a mountain in the wilderness of Ziph. And Saul sought him every day, but God delivered him not into his hand. <hi type="super">15</hi> And David saw that Saul was come out to seek his life: and David <hi type="italic">was</hi> in the wilderness of Ziph in a wood. <hi type="super">16</hi> And Jonathan Saul's son arose, and went to David into the wood, and strengthened his hand in God. <hi type="super">17</hi> And he said unto him, Fear not: for the hand of Saul my father shall not find thee; and thou shalt be king over Israel, and I shall be next unto thee; and that also Saul my father knoweth. <hi type="super">18</hi> And they two made a covenant before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : and David abode in the wood, and Jonathan went to his house. <div eID="gen5755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5756" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. David absconding. He abode in a <hi type="italic">wilderness, in a mountain</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.23.14">v. 14</reference>), <hi type="italic">in a wood,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.15">v. 15</reference>. We must here, 1. Commend his eminent virtues, his humility, modesty, fidelity to his prince, and patient attendance on the providence of his God, that he did not draw up his forces against Saul, fight him in the field, or surprise him by some stratagem or other, and so avenge his own quarrel and that of the Lord's priests upon him, and put an end to his own troubles and the calamities of the country under Saul's tyrannical government. No, he makes no such attempt; he keeps God's way, waits God's time, and is content to secure himself in woods and wildernesses, though with some it might seem a reproach to that courage for which he had been famous. But, 2. We must also lament his hard fate, that an innocent man should be thus terrified and put in fear of his life, that a man of honour should be thus disgraced, a man of merit thus recompensed for his services, and a man that delighted in the service both of God and his country should be debarred from both and wrapped up in obscurity. What shall we say to this? Let it make us think the worse of this world, which often gives such bad treatment to its best men; let it reconcile even great and active men to privacy and restraint, if Providence make these their lot, for they were David's; and let it make us long for that kingdom where goodness shall for ever be in glory and holiness in honour, and the righteous shall shine as the sun, which cannot be put under a bushel. <div eID="gen5756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5757" type="x-p"/> II. Saul hunting him, as his implacable enemy. He sought him every day, so restless was his malice, <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.14">v. 14</reference>. He sought no less than his life, so cruel was his malice, <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.15">v. 15</reference>. As it had been from the beginning, so it was now, and will be, <hi type="italic">he that is born after the flesh persecuteth him that is born after the spirit,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gal.4.29">Gal. iv. 29</reference>. <div eID="gen5757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5758" type="x-p"/> III. God defending him, as his powerful protector. God delivered him not into Saul's hand, as Saul hoped (<reference osisRef="1Sam.23.7">v. 7</reference>); and, unless God delivered him into his hand, he could not prevail against him, <reference osisRef="John.19.11">John xix. 11</reference>. <div eID="gen5758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5759" type="x-p"/> IV. Jonathan comforting him as his faithful and constant friend. True friends will find out means to get together. David, it is likely, appointed time and place for this interview, and Jonathan observed the appointment, though he exposed himself thereby to his father's displeasure, and, had it been discovered, it might have cost him his life. True friendship will not shrink from danger, but can easily venture, will not shrink from condescension, but can easily stoop, and exchange a palace for a wood, to serve a friend. The very sight of Jonathan was reviving to David; but, besides this, he said that to him which was very encouraging. 1. As a pious friend, he directed him to God, the foundation of his confidence and the fountain of his comfort: He <hi type="italic">strengthened his hand in God.</hi> David, though a strong believer, needed the help of his friends for the perfecting of what was lacking in his faith; and herein Jonathan was helpful to him, by reminding him of the promise of God, the holy oil wherewith he was anointed, the presence of God with him hitherto, and the many experiences he had had of God's goodness to him. Thus he strengthened his hands for action, by encouraging his heart, not in the creature, but in God. Jonathan was not in a capacity of doing any thing to strengthen him, but he assured him God would. 2. As a self-denying friend, he took a pleasure in the prospect of David's advancement to that honour which was his own birthright, <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.17">v. 17</reference>. "Thou shalt live to be king, and I shall think it preferment enough to be next thee, near thee, though under thee, and will never pretend to be a rival with thee." This resignation which Jonathan made to David of his title would be a great satisfaction to him, and make his way much the more clear. This, he tells him, Saul knew very well, Jonathan having sometimes heard him say as much, whence it appears what a wicked man Saul was, to persecute one whom God favoured, and what a foolish man he was, in thinking to prevent that which God had determined and which would certainly come to pass. How could he disannul what God had purposed? 3. As a constant friend, he renewed his league of friendship with him. They made a covenant now, this third time, before the Lord, calling him to witness to it, <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.18">v. 18</reference>. True love takes delight in repeating its engagements, giving and receiving fresh assurances of the firmness of the friendship. Our covenant with God should be often renewed, and therein our communion with him kept up. David and Jonathan now parted, and never came together again, that we find, in this world; for Jonathan said what he wished, not what he had ground to expect, when he promised himself that he should be next to David in his kingdom.
entries.3c170263c6d8c6e4320b2904ac334fae57302e26: <div eID="gen5759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5760" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> Then came up the Ziphites to Saul to Gibeah, saying, Doth not David hide himself with us in strong holds in the wood, in the hill of Hachilah, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> on the south of Jeshimon? <hi type="super">20</hi> Now therefore, O king, come down according to all the desire of thy soul to come down; and our part <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> to deliver him into the king's hand. <hi type="super">21</hi> And Saul said, Blessed <hi type="italic">be</hi> ye of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; for ye have compassion on me. <hi type="super">22</hi> Go, I pray you, prepare yet, and know and see his place where his haunt is, <hi type="italic">and</hi> who hath seen him there: for it is told me <hi type="italic">that</hi> he dealeth very subtilly. <hi type="super">23</hi> See therefore, and take knowledge of all the lurking places where he hideth himself, and come ye again to me with the certainty, and I will go with you: and it shall come to pass, if he be in the land, that I will search him out throughout all the thousands of Judah. <hi type="super">24</hi> And they arose, and went to Ziph before Saul: but David and his men <hi type="italic">were</hi> in the wilderness of Maon, in the plain on the south of Jeshimon. <hi type="super">25</hi> Saul also and his men went to seek <hi type="italic">him.</hi> And they told David: wherefore he came down into a rock, and abode in the wilderness of Maon. And when Saul heard <hi type="italic">that,</hi> he pursued after David in the wilderness of Maon. <hi type="super">26</hi> And Saul went on this side of the mountain, and David and his men on that side of the mountain: and David made haste to get away for fear of Saul; for Saul and his men compassed David and his men round about to take them. <hi type="super">27</hi> But there came a messenger unto Saul, saying, Haste thee, and come; for the Philistines have invaded the land. <hi type="super">28</hi> Wherefore Saul returned from pursuing after David, and went against the Philistines: therefore they called that place Sela-hammahlekoth. <hi type="super">29</hi> And David went up from thence, and dwelt in strong holds at En-gedi. <div eID="gen5760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5761" type="x-p"/> Here, 1. The Ziphites offer their service to Saul, to betray David to him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.19-1Sam.23.20">v. 19, 20</reference>. He was sheltering himself in the wilderness of Ziph (<reference osisRef="1Sam.23.14-1Sam.23.15">v. 14, 15</reference>), putting the more confidence in the people of that country because they were of his own tribe. They had reason to think themselves happy that they had an opportunity of serving one who was the ornament of their tribe and was likely to be much more so, who was so far from plundering the country, or giving it any disturbance with his troops, that he was ready to protect it and to them all the good offices that there was occasion for. But, to ingratiate themselves with Saul, they went to him, and not only informed him very particularly where David quartered (<reference osisRef="1Sam.23.19">v. 19</reference>), but invited him to come with his forces into their country in pursuit of him, and promised to deliver him into his hand, <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.20">v. 20</reference>. Saul had not sent to examine or threaten them, but of their own accord, and even without asking a reward (as Judas did—<hi type="italic">What will you give me?</hi>), they offered to betray David to him who, they knew, thirsted after his blood. 2. Saul thankfully receives their information, and gladly lays hold of the opportunity of hunting David in their wilderness, in hopes to make a prey of him at length. He intimates to them how kindly he took it (<reference osisRef="1Sam.23.21">v. 21</reference>): <hi type="italic">Blessed be you of the Lord</hi> (so near is God to his mouth, though far from his heart), <hi type="italic">for you have compassion on me.</hi> It seems he looked upon himself as a miserable man and an object of pity; his own envy and ill-nature made him so, otherwise he might have been easy and have needed no man's compassion. He likewise insinuates the little concern that the generality of his people showed for him. "You have compassion on me, which others have not." Saul gives them instructions to search more particularly for his haunts (<reference osisRef="1Sam.23.22">v. 22</reference>), "for" (says he) "I hear he deals very subtilely," representing him as a man crafty to do mischief, whereas all his subtlety was to secure himself. It was strange that Saul did not go down with them immediately, but he hoped by their means to set his game with the more certainty, and thus divine Providence gave David time to shift for himself. But the Ziphites had laid their spies upon all the places where he was likely to be discovered, and therefore Saul might come and seize him if he was in the land, <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.23">v. 23</reference>. Now he thought himself sure of his prey and pleased himself with the thoughts of devouring it. 3. The imminent peril that David was now brought into. Upon intelligence that the Ziphites had betrayed him, he retired from the hill of Hachilah to the wilderness of Maon (<reference osisRef="1Sam.23.24">v. 24</reference>), and at this time he penned the <reference osisRef="Ps.54.1-Ps.54.7">54th Psalm</reference>, as appears by the title, wherein he calls the Ziphites <hi type="italic">strangers,</hi> though they were Israelites, because they used him barbarously; but he puts himself under the divine protection: "<hi type="italic">Behold, God is my helper,</hi> and then all shall be well" Saul, having got intelligence of him, pursued him closely (<reference osisRef="1Sam.23.25">v. 25</reference>), till he came so near him that there was but a mountain between them (<reference osisRef="1Sam.23.26">v. 26</reference>), David and his men on one side of the mountain flying and Saul and his men on the other side pursuing, David in fear and Saul in hope. But this mountain was an emblem of the divine Providence coming between David and the destroyer, like the pillar of cloud between the Israelites and the Egyptians. David was concealed by this mountain and Saul confounded by it. David now flees <hi type="italic">as a bird to his mountain</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.11.1">Ps. xi. 1</reference>) and finds God to him as the shadow of a great rock. Saul hoped with his numerous forces to enclose David, and compass him in and his men; but the ground did not prove convenient for his design, and so it failed. A new name was given to the place in remembrance of this (<reference osisRef="1Sam.23.28">v. 28</reference>): <hi type="italic">Selah-hammah-lekoth—the rock of division,</hi> because it divided between Saul and David. 4. The deliverance of David out of this danger. Providence gave Saul a diversion, when he was just ready to lay hold of David; notice was brought him that the Philistines were <hi type="italic">invading the land</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.23.27">v. 27</reference>), probably that part of the land where his own estate lay, which would be seized, or at least spoiled, by the invaders; for the little notice he took of Keilah's distress and David's relief of it, in the beginning of this chapter, gives us cause to suspect that he would not now have left pursuing David, and gone to oppose the Philistines, if some private interests of his own had not been at stake. However it was, he found himself under a necessity of <hi type="italic">going against the Philistines</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Sam.23.28">v. 28</reference>), and by this means David was delivered when he was on the brink of destruction. Saul was disappointed of his prey, and God was glorified as David's wonderful protector. When the Philistines invaded the land they were far from intending any kindness to David by it, yet the overruling providence of God, which orders all events and the times of them, made it very serviceable to him. The wisdom of God is never at a loss for ways and means to preserve his people. As this Saul was diverted, so another Saul was converted, just then when he was <hi type="italic">breathing out threatenings and slaughter against the saints of the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.9.1">Acts ix. 1</reference>. 5. David, having thus escaped, took shelter in some natural fortresses, which he found in the wilderness of En-gedi, <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.29">v. 29</reference>. And this Dr. Lightfoot thinks was the wilderness of Judah, in which David was when he penned <reference osisRef="Ps.63.1-Ps.63.11">Psalm 63</reference>, which breathes as much pious and devout affection as almost any of his psalms; for in all places and in all conditions he still kept up his communion with God.  <chapter eID="1Sam.23"/> <div eID="gen5761" type="x-p"/>

entries.409cfee3483ff5527434413cc6ec11b2b0670f4c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2745"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 23</title> <div sID="gen3749" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.1-1Sam.23.6">1Sa 23:1-6</reference>. David Rescues Keilah.<div eID="gen3749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3750" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2745"/><hi type="bold">1. Then they told David--</hi>rather, "now they had told"; for this information had reached him previous to his hearing (<reference osisRef="1Sam.23.6">1Sa 23:6</reference>) of the Nob tragedy.<div eID="gen3750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3751" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Keilah--</hi>a city in the west of Judah (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.44">Jos 15:44</reference>), not far from the forest of Hareth.<div eID="gen3751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3752" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and they rob the threshing-floors--</hi>These were commonly situated on the fields and were open to the wind (<reference osisRef="Judg.6.11">Jud 6:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ruth.3.2">Ru 3:2</reference>). <div eID="gen3752" type="x-p"/>
entries.7e4ed3b6697d4cd63e3c6a0da6345a8622f8f057: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2746"/><div sID="gen3753" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2746"/><hi type="bold">2-5. David inquired of the Lord--</hi>most probably through Gad (<reference osisRef="2Sam.24.11">2Sa 24:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.21.9">1Ch 21:9</reference>), who was present in David's camp (<reference osisRef="1Sam.22.5">1Sa 22:5</reference>), probably by the recommendation of Samuel. To repel unprovoked assaults on unoffending people who were engaged in their harvest operations, was a humane and benevolent service. But it was doubtful how far it was David's duty to go against a public enemy without the royal commission; and on that account he asked, and obtained, the divine counsel. A demur on the part of his men led David to renew the consultation for their satisfaction; after which, being fully assured of his duty, he encountered the aggressors and, by a signal victory, delivered the people of Keilah from further molestation. <div eID="gen3753" type="x-p"/>
entries.6be0a08827e015e6869357cfe7ca05c702bfdf26: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2747"/><div sID="gen3754" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2747"/><hi type="bold">6. an ephod--</hi>in which was the Urim and Thummim (<reference osisRef="Exod.28.30">Ex 28:30</reference>). It had, probably, been committed to his care, while Ahimelech and the other priests repaired to Gibeah, in obedience to the summons of Saul.<div eID="gen3754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3755" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.7-1Sam.23.13">1Sa 23:7-13</reference>. Saul's Coming, and Treachery of the Keilites. <div eID="gen3755" type="x-p"/>
entries.8aa3a7265072c1fd6d630b6410ebb0a0f2775c41: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2748"/><div sID="gen3756" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2748"/><hi type="bold">7. it was told Saul that David was come to Keilah--</hi>Saul imagined himself now certain of his victim, who would be hemmed within a fortified town. The wish was father to the thought. How wonderfully slow and unwilling to be convinced by all his experience, that the special protection of Providence shielded David from all his snares! <div eID="gen3756" type="x-p"/>
entries.b68b7b237701e2f385f24659be7f8b0fd86f83b7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2749"/><div sID="gen3757" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2749"/><hi type="bold">8. Saul called all the people together to war--</hi>not the united tribes of Israel, but the inhabitants of the adjoining districts. This force was raised, probably, on the ostensible pretext of opposing the Philistines, while, in reality, it was secretly to arouse mischief against David. <div eID="gen3757" type="x-p"/>
entries.11eaa87d3de42293b22dd51f166cf272001ef004: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2750"/><div sID="gen3758" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2750"/><hi type="bold">9. he said to Abiathar the priest, Bring hither the ephod--</hi>The consultation was made, and the prayer uttered, by means of the priest. The alternative conditions here described have often been referred to as illustrating the doctrine of God's foreknowledge and preordination of events.<div eID="gen3758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3759" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.14-1Sam.23.18">1Sa 23:14-18</reference>. David Escapes to Ziph. <div eID="gen3759" type="x-p"/>
entries.d682deff10f45dec1d2fd9cce8f7068506f62edb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2751"/><div sID="gen3760" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2751"/><hi type="bold">14-15. David abode in the wilderness ... of Ziph--</hi>A mountainous and sequestered region was generally called a wilderness, and took its name from some large town in the district. Two miles southeast of Hebron, and in the midst of a level plain, is Tell-ziph, an isolated and conical hillock, about a hundred feet high, probably the acropolis [Van De Velde], or the ruins [Robinson] of the ancient city of Ziph, from which the surrounding wilderness was called. It seems, anciently, to have been covered by an extensive woods. The country has for centuries lost its woods and forests, owing to the devastations caused by man. <div eID="gen3760" type="x-p"/>
entries.55412f5503760a288df4ffa7fec4c4ed63a3a4b7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2752"/><div sID="gen3761" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2752"/><hi type="bold">16-17. Jonathan went to David into the wood, and strengthened his hand in God--</hi>by the recollection of their mutual covenant. What a victory over natural feelings and lower considerations must the faith of Jonathan have won, before he could seek such an interview and give utterance to such sentiments! To talk with calm and assured confidence of himself and family being superseded by the man who was his friend by the bonds of a holy and solemn covenant, could only have been done by one who, superior to all views of worldly policy, looked at the course of things in the spirit and through the principles of that theocracy which acknowledged God as the only and supreme Sovereign of Israel. Neither history nor fiction depicts the movements of a friendship purer, nobler, and more self-denying than Jonathan's!<div eID="gen3761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3762" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.19-1Sam.23.29">1Sa 23:19-29</reference>. Saul Pursues Him. <div eID="gen3762" type="x-p"/>
entries.ceabc901121d1f294c7dba86a10a3c76e3dbbb5d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2753"/><div sID="gen3763" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2753"/><hi type="bold">19-23. Then came up the Ziphites to Saul to Gibeah, saying, Doth not David hide himself with us?--</hi>From the tell of Ziph a panorama of the whole surrounding district is to be seen. No wonder, then, that the Ziphites saw David and his men passing to and fro in the mountains of the wilderness. Spying him at a distance when he ventured to show himself on the hill of Hachilah, "on the right hand of the wilderness," that is, the south side of Ziph, they sent in haste to Saul, to tell him of the lurking place of his enemy [Van De Velde]. <div eID="gen3763" type="x-p"/>
entries.f6fbfb2481764af7c0a38f7c72610e4c8f5ff5cb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2754"/><div sID="gen3764" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2754"/><hi type="bold">25. David ... came down into a rock, and abode in the wilderness of Maon--</hi>Tell Main, the hillock on which was situated the ancient Maon (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.55">Jos 15:55</reference>), and from which the adjoining wilderness took its name, is one mile north, ten east from Carmel. The mountain plateau seems here to end. It is true the summit ridge of the southern hills runs out a long way further towards the southwest; but towards the southeast the ground sinks more and more down to a tableland of a lower level, which is called "the plain to the right hand [that is, to the south] of the wilderness" [Van De Velde]. <div eID="gen3764" type="x-p"/>
entries.34b7f8da62abed1f6ad2dd5e8eb72047ebbc5e9e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2755"/><div sID="gen3765" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2755"/><hi type="bold">29. David went up from thence, and dwelt in strong holds at En-gedi--</hi>that is, "the spring of the wild goats or gazelles"--a name given to it from the vast number of ibexes or Syrian chamois which inhabit these cliffs on the western shore of the Dead Sea (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.62">Jos 15:62</reference>). It is now called Ain Jiddy. On all sides the country is full of caverns, which might then serve as lurking places for David and his men, as they do for outlaws at the present day [Robinson]. <chapter eID="1Sam.23"/>

entries.0e26b3a401ec36e82841540b8473cc17e64f6140: <div eID="gen10356" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen10357" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10358" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10358" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10357" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10359" type="x-p"/> David succours Keilah, besieged by the Philistines; defeats them, and delivers the city, <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.1-1Sam.23.6">1Sam 23:1-6</reference>. Saul, hearing that David was at Keilah, determines to come and seize him, <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.7">1Sam 23:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.8">1Sam 23:8</reference>. David inquires of the Lord concerning the fidelity of the men of Keilah towards him; is informed that if he stays in the city, the men of Keilah will betray him to Saul, <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.9-1Sam.23.12">1Sam 23:9-12</reference>. David and his men escape from the city, and come to the wilderness of Ziph, <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.13-1Sam.23.15">1Sam 23:13-15</reference>. Jonathan meets David in the wood of Ziph, strengthens his hand in God, and they renew their covenant, <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.16-1Sam.23.18">1Sam 23:16-18</reference>. The Ziphites endeavor to betray David to Saul, but he and his men escape to Maon, <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.19-1Sam.23.22">1Sam 23:19-22</reference>. Saul comes to Maon; and having surrounded the mountain on which David and his men were, they must inevitably have fallen into his hands, had not a messenger come to call Saul to the succor of Judah, then invaded by the Philistines, <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.25-1Sam.23.27">1Sam 23:25-27</reference>. Saul leaves the pursuit of David, and goes to succor the land; and David escapes to En-gedi, <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.28">1Sam 23:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.29">1Sam 23:29</reference>. <div eID="gen10359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10360" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen10360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10361" type="x-p"/> The Philistines fight against Keilah - Keilah was a fortified town in the tribe of Judah near to Eleutheropolis, on the road to Hebron. <div eID="gen10361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10362" type="x-p"/> Rob the threshing-floors - This was an ancient custom of the Philistines, Midianites, and others. See <reference osisRef="Jdg.6.4">Jdg 6:4</reference>. When the corn was ripe and fit to be threshed, and they had collected it at the threshing-floors, which were always in the open field, then their enemies came upon them and spoiled them of the fruits of their harvest.
entries.5bfd9784ee01e039280ad7dd492309d05d4e9a99: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen10362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10363" type="x-p"/> Therefore David inquired of the Lord - In what way David made this inquiry we are not told, but it was probably by means of Abiathar; and therefore I think, with Houbigant that the sixth verse should be read immediately after the first. The adventure mentioned here was truly noble. Had not David loved his country, and been above all motives of private and personal revenge, he would have rejoiced in this invasion of Judah as producing a strong diversion in his favor, and embroiling his inveterate enemy. In most cases a man with David's wrongs would have joined with the enemies of his country, and avenged himself on the author of his adversities; but he thinks of nothing but succouring Keilah, and using his power and influence in behalf of his brethren! This is a rare instance of disinterested heroism. <div eID="gen10363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10364" type="x-p"/> The Lord said - Go and smite - He might now go with confidence, being assured of success. When God promises success, who need be afraid of the face of any enemy?
entries.718d9f41993adb9663fde8ee668181d4bc3593ee: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen10364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10365" type="x-p"/> David inquired of the Lord yet again - This was to satisfy his men, who made the strong objections mentioned in the preceding verse.
entries.b41a4d05b95411b819959b65b8d2b5de053511af: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen10365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10366" type="x-p"/> Brought away their cattle - The forage and spoil which the Philistines had taken, driving the country before them round about Keilah.
entries.17f3637d0fd32812a4621f19646f70caf5f55b38: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen10366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10367" type="x-p"/> Came down with an ephod - I think this verse should come immediately after <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.1">1Sam 23:1</reference> (note).
entries.64d98182b039206daba27dd69e8e4a292f10af05: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen10367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10368" type="x-p"/> Saul called all the people together - That is, all the people of that region or district, that they might scour the country, and hunt out David from all his haunts.
entries.c616d59b9d83d4cc94ce799b0311968d4fc987e5: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen10368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10369" type="x-p"/> Bring hither the ephod - It seems as if David himself, clothed with the ephod, had consulted the Lord; and <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.10-1Sam.23.12">1Sam 23:10-12</reference> contain the words of the consultation, and the Lord's answer. But see on <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.2">1Sam 23:2</reference> (note).
entries.f3ef6416de35dfcf9745702aed4db339e2a0da99: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen10369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10370" type="x-p"/> In these verses we find the following questions and answers: - David said, Will Saul come down to Keilah? And the Lord said, He will come down. Will the men of Keilah deliver me and my men into the hand of Saul? And the Lord said, They will deliver thee up. In this short history we find an ample proof that there is such a thing as contingency in human affairs; that is, God has poised many things between a possibility of being and not being, leaving it to the will of the creature to turn the scale. In the above answers of the Lord the following conditions were evidently implied: - If thou continue in Keilah, Saul will certainly come down; and If Saul come down, the men of Keilah will deliver thee into his hands. Now though the text positively asserts that Saul would come to Keilah, yet he did not come; and that the men of Keilah would deliver David into his hand, yet David was not thus delivered to him. And why? Because David left Keilah; but had he stayed, Saul would have come down, and the men of Keilah would have betrayed David. We may observe from this that, however positive a declaration of God may appear that refers to any thing in which man is to be employed, the prediction is not intended to suspend or destroy free agency, but always comprehends in it some particular condition.
entries.655677d4892c670f32198079099e08b8f8e53574: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen10370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10371" type="x-p"/> Wilderness of Ziph - Ziph was a city in the southern part of Judea, not far from Carmel.
entries.3c6f67ca0e41246f672904ce68347a3ba46c2ea6: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen10371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10372" type="x-p"/> And Jonathan - strengthened his hand in God - It is probable that there was always a secret intercourse between David and Jonathan, and that by this most trusty friend he was apprised of the various designs of Saul to take away his life. As Jonathan well knew that God had appointed David to the kingdom, he came now to encourage him to trust in the Most High, and to assure him that the hand of Saul should not prevail against him; and at this interview they renewed their covenant of friendship. Now all this Jonathan could do, consistently with his duty to his father and his king. He knew that David had delivered the kingdom; he saw that his father was ruling unconstitutionally; and he knew that God had appointed David to succeed Saul. This he knew would come about in the order of Providence; and neither he nor David took one step to hasten the time. Jonathan, by his several interferences, prevented his father from imbruing his hands in innocent blood: a more filial and a more loyal part he could not have acted; and therefore, in his attachment to David, he is wholly free of blame.
entries.d3d0ca8bd6693ad226be33eae9d001b6d2e3e7d9: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen10372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10373" type="x-p"/> The wilderness of Maon - Maon was a mountainous district in the most southern parts of Judah. Calmet supposes it to be the city of Menois, which Eusebius places in the vicinity of Gaza; and the Maenaemi Castrum, which the Theodosian code places near to Beersheba.
entries.8907830f5cc7b9ebf028faf5c3b85758c0c8f9f2: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen10373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10374" type="x-p"/> Saul went on this side of the mountain - Evidently not knowing that David and his men were on the other side.
entries.f0e3799d596dd7b2d20c81b8caf18675532b8f97: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen10374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10375" type="x-p"/> There came a messenger - See the providence of God exerted for the salvation of David's life! David and his men are almost surrounded by Saul and his army, and on the point of being taken, when a messenger arrives and informs Saul that the Philistines had invaded the land! But behold the workings of Providence! God had already prepared the invasion of the land by the Philistines, and kept Saul ignorant how much David was in his power; but as his advanced guards and scouts must have discovered him in a very short time, the messenger arrives just at the point of time to prevent it. Here David was delivered by God, and in such a manner too as rendered the Divine interposition visible.
entries.4f6827d04f4624a15d84005e1fe79664e8b941e4: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen10375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10376" type="x-p"/> They called that place Sela-hammah-lekoth - That is, the rock of divisions; because, says the Targum, the heart of the king was divided to go hither and thither. Here Saul was obliged to separate himself from David, in order to go and oppose the invading Philistines.
entries.e64e77321be267d69b1552cf49613d42ac5b6d4d: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen10376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10377" type="x-p"/> Strong holds at En-gedi - En-gedi was situated near to the western coast of the Dead Sea, not far from Jeshimon: it literally signifies the kid's well, and was celebrated for its vineyards, <reference osisRef="Sol.1.14">Sol 1:14</reference>. It was also celebrated for its balm. It is reported to be a mountainous territory, filled with caverns; and consequently proper for David in his present circumstances. <div eID="gen10377" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10378" type="x-p"/> How threshing-floors were made among the ancients, we learn from Cato, De Re Rustica, chap. 91, and 129. And as I believe it would be an excellent method to make the most durable and efficient barn-floors, I will set it down: - Aream sic facito. Locum ubi facies confodito; postea amurca conspergito bene, sinitoque combibat. Postea comminuito glebas bene. Deinde coaequato, et paviculis verberato. Postea denuo amurca conspergito, sinitoque arescat. Si ita feceris neque formicae nocebunt, neque herbae nascentur: et cum pluerit, lutum non erit. "Make a threshing-floor thus: dig the place thoroughly; afterwards sprinkle it well with the lees of oil, and give it time to soak in. Then beat the clods very fine, make it level, and beat it well down with a paver's rammer. When this is done, sprinkle it afresh with the oil lees, and let it dry. This being done, the mice cannot burrow in it, no grass can grow through it, nor will the rain dissolve the surface to raise mud." <div eID="gen10378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10379" type="x-p"/> The directions of Columella are nearly the same; but as there as some differences of importance, I will subjoin his account: - <div eID="gen10379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10380" type="x-p"/> Area quoque si terrena erit, ut sit ad trituram satis habilis, primum radatur, deinde confodiatur, permixtis paleis cum amurca, quae salem non accepit, extergatur; nam ea res a populatione murium formicarumque frumenta defendit. Tum aequate paviculis, vel molari lapide condensetur, et rursus subjectis paleis inculcetur, atque ita solibus siccanda relinquatur. <div eID="gen10380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10381" type="x-p"/> De Re Rustica, lib. ii., c. 20. "If you would have a threshing-floor made on the open ground, that it may be proper for the purpose, first pare off the surface, then let it be well digged, and mixed with lees of oil, unsalted, with which chaff has been mingled, for this prevents the mice and ants from burrowing and injuring the corn. Then level it with a paver's rammer, or press it down with a millstone. Afterwards scatter chaff over it, tread it down, and leave it to be dried by the sun." <div eID="gen10381" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10382" type="x-p"/> This may be profitably used within doors, as well as in the field; and a durable and solid floor is a matter of very great consequence to the husbandman, as it prevents the flour from being injured by sand or dust.  <chapter eID="1Sam.23"/> <div eID="gen10382" type="x-p"/>

entries.5339679b3bc27d81253bd1ddeaf00ed3eec4056b: <div eID="gen4059" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">David Delivers Keilah. He Is Betrayed by the Ziphites, and Marvellously Saved from Saul in the Desert of Maon - 1 Samuel 23</title> <div sID="gen4060" type="x-p"/> The following events show how, on the one hand, the Lord gave pledges to His servant David that he would eventually become king, but yet on the other hand plunged him into deeper and deeper trouble, that He might refine him and train him to be a king after His own heart. Saul’s rage against the priests at Nob not only drove the high priest into David’s camp, but procured for David the help of the “light and right” of the high priest in all his undertakings. Moreover, after the prophet Gad had called David back to Judah, an attack of the Philistines upon Keilah furnished him with the opportunity to show himself to the people as their deliverer. And although this enterprise of his exposed him to fresh persecutions on the part of Saul, who was thirsting for revenge, he experienced in connection therewith not only the renewal of Jonathan’s friendship on this occasion, but a marvellous interposition on the part of the faithful covenant God. <div eID="gen4060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4061" type="x-p"/> Rescue of Keilah. - After his return to the mountains of Judah, David received intelligence that Philistines, i.e., a marauding company of these enemies of Israel, were fighting against Keilah, and plundering the threshing-floors, upon which the corn that had been reaped was lying ready for threshing. <hi type="italic">Keilah</hi> belonged to the towns of the lowlands of Judah (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.44">Jos 15:44</reference>); and although it has not yet been discovered, was certainly very close to the Philistian frontier.
entries.654aa66281a17b7628b7f0641dc7a619660e8e65: <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.2">1Sa 23:2</reference> <div eID="gen4061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4062" type="x-p"/> After receiving this information, David inquired of the Lord (through the Urim and Thummim of the high priest) whether he should go and smite these Philistines, and received an affirmative answer.
entries.dc8c9b7a1ed3b71a9f3981e92c6aa60c58af15d9: <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.3-1Sam.23.6">1Sa 23:3-6</reference> <div eID="gen4062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4063" type="x-p"/> But his men said to him, “<hi type="italic">Behold, here in Judah we are in fear</hi> (i.e., are not safe from Saul’s pursuit); <hi type="italic">how shall we go to Keilah against the ranks of the Philistines?</hi>” In order, therefore, to infuse courage into them, he inquired of the Lord again, and received the assurance from God, “<hi type="italic">I will give the Philistines into thy hand</hi>.” He then proceeded with his men, fought against the Philistines, drove off their cattle, inflicted a severe defeat upon them, and thus delivered the inhabitants of Keilah. In <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.6">1Sa 23:6</reference> a supplementary remark is added in explanation of the expression “<hi type="italic">inquired of the Lord</hi>,” to the effect that, when Abiathar fled to David to Keilah, the ephod had come to him. The words “<hi type="italic">to David to Keilah</hi>” are not to be understood as signifying that Abiathar did not come to David till he was in Keilah, but that when he fled after David (<reference osisRef="1Sam.22.20">1Sa 22:20</reference>), he met with him as he was already preparing for the march of Keilah, and immediately proceeded with him thither. For whilst it is not stated in <reference osisRef="1Sam.22.20">1Sa 22:20</reference> that Abiathar came to David in the wood of Hareth, but the place of meeting is left indefinite, the fact that David had already inquired of Jehovah (i.e., through the oracle of the high priest) with reference to the march to Keilah, compels us to assume that Abiathar had come to him before he left the mountains for Keilah. So that the brief expression “to David to Keilah,” which is left indefinite because of its brevity, must be interpreted in accordance with this fact.
entries.2c35ce51e5ae81b9417c304aab2cdaa3bc35145a: <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.7-1Sam.23.9">1Sa 23:7-9</reference> <div eID="gen4063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4064" type="x-p"/> As soon as Saul received intelligence of David’s march to Keilah, he said, “<hi type="italic">God has rejected him</hi> (and delivered him) <hi type="italic">into my hand</hi>.” נכּר does not mean simply to look at, but also to find strange, and treat as strange, and then absolutely to <hi type="italic">reject</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.19.4">Jer 19:4</reference>, as in the Arabic in the fourth conjugation). This is the meaning here, where the construction with בּידי is to be understood as a pregnant expression: “<hi type="italic">rejection and delivered into my hand</hi>” (vid., <hi type="italic">Ges.</hi> <hi type="italic">Lex. s. v.</hi>). The early translators have rendered it quite correctly according to the sense מכר, πέπρακεν, <hi type="italic">tradidit</hi>, without there being any reason to suppose that they read מכר instead of נכּר. “<hi type="italic">For he hath shut himself in, to come</hi> (= coming, or by coming) <hi type="italic">into a city with gates and bolts</hi>.”
entries.8d236123bf38e8bac91c8a5428fcf9d9856b00a0: <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.13">1Sa 23:13</reference> <div eID="gen4066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4067" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">They went whithersoever they could go</hi>” (<hi type="italic">lit</hi>. “they wandered about where they wandered about”), i.e., wherever they could go without danger.
entries.cddb4c73a62e41bd7b3ddab80ca7ee9803be92d6: <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.14">1Sa 23:14</reference> <div eID="gen4067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4068" type="x-p"/> David retreated into the desert (of Judah), to the mountain heights (that were to be found there), and remained on the mountains in the desert of Ziph. The “<hi type="italic">desert of Judah</hi>” is the desert tract between the mountains of Judah and the Dead Sea, in its whole extent, from the northern boundary of the tribe of Judah to the Wady Fikreh in the south (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.15.61">Jos 15:61</reference>). Certain portions of this desert, however, received different names of their own, according to the names of different towns on the border of the mountains and desert. The desert of <hi type="italic">Ziph</hi> was that portion of the desert of Judah which was near to and surrounded the town of <hi type="italic">Ziph</hi>, the name of which has been retained in the ruins of <hi type="italic">Tell Zif</hi>, an hour and three-quarters to the south-east of Hebron (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.15.55">Jos 15:55</reference>).<hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="1Sam.23.14">1Sa 23:14</reference></hi>. “And Saul sought him all the days, but God delivered him not into his hand.” This is a general remark, intended to introduce the accounts which follow, of the various attempts made by Saul to get David into his power. “<hi type="italic">All the days</hi>,” i.e., as long as Saul lived.
entries.8ebdbdcb0ff79b563f59fb17d6ba0c8d42fdbb9a: <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.15-1Sam.23.17">1Sa 23:15-17</reference> <div eID="gen4068" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4069" type="x-p"/> David in the Deserts of Ziph and Maon. - The history of David’s persecution by Saul is introduced in <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.15-1Sam.23.18">1Sa 23:15-18</reference>, with the account of an attempt made by the noble-minded prince Jonathan, in a private interview with his friend David, to renew his bond of friendship with him, and strengthen David by his friendly words for the sufferings that yet awaited him. <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.15">1Sa 23:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.16">1Sa 23:16</reference> are to be connected together so as to form one period: “<hi type="italic">When David saw that Saul was come out ... and David was in the desert of Ziph, Jonathan rose up and went to David into the wood</hi>.” חרשׁה, from חרשׁ, with ה paragogic, signifies a wood or thicket; here, however, it is probably a proper name for a district in the desert of Ziph that was overgrown with wood or bushes, and where David was stopping at that time. “There is no trace of this wood now. The land lost its ornament of trees centuries ago through the desolating hand of man” (v. de Velde). “<hi type="italic">And strengthened his hand in God</hi>,” i.e., strengthened his heart, not by supplies, or by money, or any subsidy of that kind, but by consolation drawn from his innocence, and the promises of God (vid., Jdg 9:24; <reference osisRef="Jer.23.14">Jer 23:14</reference>). “<hi type="italic">Fear not</hi>,” said Jonathan to him, “<hi type="italic">for the hand of Saul my father will not reach thee; and thou wilt become king over Israel, and I will be the second to thee; and Saul my father also knows that it is so</hi>.” Even though Jonathan had heard nothing from David about his anointing, he could learn from David’s course thus far, and from his own father’s conduct, that David would not be overcome, but would possess the sovereignty after the death of Saul. Jonathan expresses here, as his firm conviction, what he has intimated once before, in 1Sa 20:13.; and with the most loving self-denial entreats David, when he shall be king, to let him occupy the second place in the kingdom. It by no means follows from the last words (“<hi type="italic">Saul my father knoweth</hi>”), that Saul had received distinct information concerning the anointing of David, and his divine calling to be king. The words merely contain the thought, he also sees that it will come. The assurance of this must have forced itself involuntarily upon the mind of Saul, both from his own rejection, as foretold by Samuel, and also from the marvellous success of David in all his undertakings.
entries.c4552c60ad56c034f61554751763bbaf64c20983: <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.18-1Sam.23.20">1Sa 23:18-20</reference> <div eID="gen4069" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4070" type="x-p"/> After these encouraging words, they two made a covenant before Jehovah: i.e., they renewed the covenant which they had already made by another solemn oath; after which Jonathan returned home, but David remained in the wood. <div eID="gen4070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4071" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">treachery of the Ziphites</hi> forms a striking contrast to Jonathan’s treatment of David. They went up to Gibeah to betray to Saul the fact that David was concealed in the wood upon their mountain heights, and indeed “<hi type="italic">upon the hill Hachilah, which lies to the south of the waste</hi>.” The hill of <hi type="italic">Ziph</hi> is a flattened hill standing by itself, of about a hundred feet in height. “There is no spot from which you can obtain a better view of David’s wanderings backwards and forwards in the desert than from the hill of <hi type="italic">Ziph</hi>, which affords a true panorama. The Ziphites could see David and his men moving to and fro in the mountains of the desert of <hi type="italic">Ziph</hi>, and could also perceive how he showed himself in the distance upon the hill <hi type="italic">Hachilah</hi> on the south side of <hi type="italic">Ziph</hi> (which lies to the right by the desert); whereupon they sent as quickly as possible to Saul, and betrayed to him the hiding-place of his enemy” (v. de Velde, ii. pp. 104-5). <hi type="italic">Jeshimon</hi> does not refer here to the waste land on the north-eastern coast of the Dead Sea, as in Num 21:20; Num 23:28, but to the western side of that sea, which is also desert. <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.20">1Sa 23:20</reference> reads literally thus: “<hi type="italic">And now, according to all the desire of thy soul, O king, to come down </hi>(from Gibeah, which stood upon higher ground), <hi type="italic">come down, and it is in us to deliver him</hi> (David) <hi type="italic">into the hand of the king</hi>.”
entries.3324f694b6511445a80d5ec95667d57876959202: <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.21">1Sa 23:21</reference> <div eID="gen4071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4072" type="x-p"/> For this treachery Saul blessed them: “<hi type="italic">Be blessed of the Lord, that ye have compassion upon me</hi>.” In his evil conscience he suspected David of seeking to become his murderer, and therefore thanked God in his delusion that the Ziphites had had compassion upon him, and shown him David’s hiding-place.
entries.43412769f691e3924b288a8ff313182a0d568860: <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.22">1Sa 23:22</reference> <div eID="gen4072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4073" type="x-p"/> In his anxiety, however, lest David should escape him after all, he charged them, “<hi type="italic">Go, and give still further heed</hi> (הכין without לב, as in Jdg 12:6), <hi type="italic">and reconnoitre and look at his place where his foot cometh</hi> (this simply serves as a more precise definition of the nominal suffix in מקומו, his place), <hi type="italic">who hath seen him there</hi> (sc., let them inquire into this, that they may not be deceived by uncertain or false reports): <hi type="italic">for it is told me that he dealeth very subtilly</hi>.”
entries.bd30fdf5ae2bdebe3fa03974196aef83d6155e6e: <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.23">1Sa 23:23</reference> <div eID="gen4073" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4074" type="x-p"/> They were to search him out in every corner (the object to דּעוּ must be supplied from the context). “<hi type="italic">And come ye again to me with the certainty</hi> (i.e., when you have got some certain intelligence concerning his hiding-place), <hi type="italic">that I may go with you; and if he is in the land, I will search him out among all the thousands</hi> (i.e., families) <hi type="italic">of Judah</hi>.”
entries.77cd438672712f230cab3ef7c59fa920f14ec3ef: <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.24">1Sa 23:24</reference> <div eID="gen4074" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4075" type="x-p"/> With this answer the Ziphites arose and “<hi type="italic">went to Ziph before Saul</hi>” (who would speedily follow with his warriors); but David had gone farther in the meantime, and was with his men “<hi type="italic">in the desert of Maon, in the steppe to the south of the wilderness</hi>.” <hi type="italic">Maon</hi>, now <hi type="italic">Maïn</hi>, is about three hours and three-quarters S.S.E. of Hebron (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.15.55">Jos 15:55</reference>), and therefore only two hours from Ziph, from which it is visible. “The table-land appears to terminate here; nevertheless the principal ridge of the southern mountains runs for a considerable distance towards the south-west, whereas towards the south-east the land falls off more and more into a lower table-land.” This is the <hi type="italic">Arabah</hi> or steppe on the right of the wilderness (v. de Velde, ii. pp. 107-8).
entries.6903e51837c69d90e3e07094cff15e934076d46e: <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.25">1Sa 23:25</reference> <div eID="gen4075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4076" type="x-p"/> Having been informed of the arrival of Saul and his men (warriors), David went down the rock, and remained in the desert of Maon. “<hi type="italic">The rock</hi>” is probably the conical mountain of <hi type="italic">Main</hi> (<hi type="italic">Maon</hi>), the top of which is now surrounded with ruins, probably remains of a tower (<hi type="italic">Robinson</hi>, <hi type="italic">Pal</hi>. ii. p. 194), as the rock from which David came down can only have been the mountain (<reference osisRef="1Sam.23.26">1Sa 23:26</reference>), along one side of which David went with his men whilst Saul and his warriors went on the other, namely when Saul pursued him into the desert of Maon.
entries.d77edec6715dfc13991a08bd0a877580febbc58f: <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.26-1Sam.23.27">1Sa 23:26-27</reference> <div eID="gen4076" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4077" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">And David was anxiously concerned to escape from Saul, and Saul and his men were encircling David and his men to seize them; but a messenger came to Saul ... . Then Saul turned from pursuing David</hi>.” The two clauses, “for Saul and his men” (<hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="1Sam.23.26">1Sa 23:26</reference></hi>), and “there came a messenger” (<reference osisRef="1Sam.23.27">1Sa 23:27</reference>), are the circumstantial clauses by which the situation is more clearly defined: the apodosis to דּוד ויהי does not follow till ויּשׁב in 1Sa 23:28. The apodosis cannot begin with וּמלאך because the verb does not stand at the head. David had thus almost inextricably fallen into the hands of Saul; but God saved him by the fact that at that very moment a messenger arrived with the intelligence, “Hasten and go (come), for Philistines have fallen into the land,” and thus called Saul away from any further pursuit of David.
entries.3b28fd76cb919920c2c75a6360b3d0f3299d85fd: <reference osisRef="1Sam.23.28">1Sa 23:28</reference> <div eID="gen4077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4078" type="x-p"/> From this occurrence the place received the name of <hi type="italic">Sela-hammahlekoth</hi>, “<hi type="italic">rock of smoothnesses</hi>,” i.e., of slipping away or escaping, from חלק, in the sense of being smooth. This explanation is at any rate better supported than “rock of divisions, i.e., the rock at which Saul and David were separated” (Clericus), since חלק does not mean to separate. Whilst Saul had gone against the Philistines, David left this dangerous place, and went to the mountain heights of <hi type="italic">Engedi</hi>, i.e., the present <hi type="italic">Ain-jidy</hi> (goat-fountain), in the middle of the western coats of the Dead Sea (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.15.62">Jos 15:62</reference>), which he could reach from Maon in six or seven hours. The soil of the neighbourhood consists entirely of limestone; but the rocks contain a considerable admixture of chalk and flint. Round about there rise bare conical mountains, and even ridges of from two to four hundred feet in height, which mostly run down to the sea. The steep mountains are intersected by wadys running down in deep ravines to the sea. “On all sides the country is full of caverns, which might then serve as lurking-places for David and his men, as they do for outlaws at the present day” (Rob. <hi type="italic">Pal</hi>. p. 203)  <chapter eID="1Sam.23"/> <div eID="gen4078" type="x-p"/>

                  <ns0:p n="10">10 Then said David <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">To wit, by the Priest, for he was to make the enqui<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry of God, <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 27. 21. and <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> puts the words into his mouth.</ns0:note>, O LORD God of Is<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rael, thy servant hath certainly heard that Saul seeketh to come to Keilah, to destroy the city for my sake.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 Will the men of Keilah deliver me up into his hand <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">To wit, if I continue in their City, and if <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> come down.</ns0:note>? Will Saul come down as thy servant hath heard? O LORD God of Israel, I beseech thee tell thy servant. And the LORD said <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">From this place it may appear that Gods answer by <ns0:hi>Urim</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Thummim,</ns0:hi> was not by any change in the co<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lour or situation of the precious Stones in the Brest-Plate of the Ephod, but by a Voice or Suggestion from God to the High-Priest.</ns0:note>, He will come down <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> He purposeth to come, if thou conti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nuest here. For still as <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s question, so Gods answer, is upon a supposition, as is here sufficiently implied.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 Then said David, Will the men of Keilah <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi>
